prompt: Why does carbon form a much wider variety of allotropes than the other group 14 elements?

choices.text: Its ability to form strong π bonds lets it build delocalized sheets (graphite, graphene) that can also wrap into tubes and balls
It is the only group 14 element that forms tetrahedral network solids
choices.why: Si and Ge also form diamond-like network covalent structures. What sets carbon apart is its strong π bonding, which allows sheet, tube and cage structures.

choices.text: Its atoms are the largest in the group, so they can pack in many ways
choices.why: Carbon's atoms are the smallest in group 14. Its small size and strong π bonds (second-row uniqueness) are what give it so many allotropes.

choices.text: It has the lowest electronegativity in the group
choices.why: Carbon has the highest electronegativity in group 14 (2.55). Its allotrope variety comes from its strong π bonding.

explanation: In keeping with the second-row uniqueness principle, carbon forms more allotropes than its heavier congeners. Its ability to form strong π bonds lets it form delocalized planar sheets (graphite and graphene), and nanotubes and fullerenes, which can be pictured as those sheets wrapped into tubes and balls.

prompt: Moving down group 14 from carbon to lead, how do the structures of the elements change?

choices.text: They become less covalent: C, Si and Ge are network covalent, tin has both network covalent and metallic forms, and lead is metallic
They become more covalent: lead forms the strongest network covalent solid
choices.why: The trend runs the other way. Covalency decreases down the group, and lead is the only group 14 element that is metallic under all conditions.

choices.text: All five elements are metals with similar structures
choices.why: Carbon, silicon and germanium are network covalent solids, not metals. Only lead is metallic in both structure and properties under all conditions.

choices.text: They alternate between metallic and covalent from one element to the next
choices.why: The change is steady, not alternating: covalent C, Si, Ge, then tin on the borderline with two forms, then metallic Pb.

explanation: There is a decreasing tendency toward covalency down the group. C, Si and Ge form network covalent structures and Pb a metallic one, while tin forms both network covalent and metallic structures that differ only slightly in stability. Lead is the only group 14 element that is metallic in both structure and properties under all conditions.

prompt: Tin has a metallic white (β) form and a gray (α) form with a diamond-like structure. What happens to white tin kept below 13.2°C?

choices.text: It converts to gray tin, the semiconducting form that is stable below 13.2°C
Nothing: white tin is the stable form at all temperatures
choices.why: White (β) tin is stable only above 13.2°C. Below that temperature the network covalent gray (α) form is the stable one.

choices.text: It converts to a metallic form like lead
choices.why: White tin is already the metallic form. Below 13.2°C it turns into gray tin, which has a diamond-like structure and is a semiconductor.

choices.text: It melts, because tin has a very low melting point
choices.why: Tin melts at 232°C. The change below 13.2°C is a solid–solid change between allotropes, from white to gray tin.

explanation: White (β) tin has a metallic lattice and metallic properties, whereas gray (α) tin has a diamond-like structure and is a semiconductor. The metallic β form is stable above 13.2°C and the nonmetallic α form is stable below 13.2°C, so white tin slowly converts to gray tin in the cold (the 'tin pest' reaction).

prompt: Why is graphite a good electrical conductor while diamond is a poor one?

choices.text: Graphite's sp2 carbons share a delocalized π bond network with a half-filled band; diamond's tetrahedral carbons are held together only by σ bonds
Graphite contains free metal impurities, while diamond is pure carbon
choices.why: Graphite's conductivity is intrinsic. It comes from its delocalized π system, which diamond, with an all-σ structure, does not have.

choices.text: Diamond's carbons are sp2 hybridized, which localizes the electrons
choices.why: It's the reverse: diamond's carbons are tetrahedral (sp3) and σ-bonded, while graphite's are trigonal planar (sp2) with delocalized π bonds.

choices.text: Graphite's layers are held together by ionic bonds that carry current
choices.why: The layers in graphite are not ionic. Conduction happens within each sheet through its delocalized π bonds.

explanation: All the carbons in a graphene sheet are trigonal planar, joined by σ overlaps of sp2 orbitals plus a delocalized π bond network. That π system involves a half-filled valence band and is responsible for graphite's good conductivity. In diamond every carbon is tetrahedral and held by σ bonds only, so, as expected from its all-σ structure, diamond is a poor conductor.

prompt: α-Graphite and β-graphite are both made of stacked graphene sheets. How do they differ?

choices.text: α-Graphite stacks the sheets in an alternating AB pattern; the slightly less stable β-graphite stacks them ABC
α-Graphite has sp3 carbons and β-graphite has sp2 carbons
choices.why: Both forms are made of the same planar sp2 graphene sheets. They differ only in how the sheets are stacked.

choices.text: In α-graphite the carbons of adjacent layers are exactly eclipsed
choices.why: In both stable graphites the layers are staggered. α-Graphite alternates them AB; β-graphite uses an ABC arrangement.

choices.text: β-Graphite is the most stable carbon allotrope
choices.why: The α form of graphite is the most stable carbon allotrope; β-graphite, with ABC stacking, is slightly less stable.

explanation: The planar graphene sheets, with π clouds above and below, can be stacked in different arrangements. The stable α-graphite has staggered layers alternating in an AB pattern, while in the slightly less stable β-graphite the layers are staggered in an ABC arrangement.

prompt: Why does graphite work well as a lubricant?

choices.text: The forces between graphene layers change little as the sheets move past one another, so the layers slip easily
The C–C bonds within each sheet are weak and break easily
choices.why: The bonds within a sheet are very strong; that is what makes graphene so strong. Lubrication comes from the layers sliding over each other.

choices.text: Graphite is a liquid at room temperature
choices.why: Graphite is a solid with an extremely high melting point. Its layers, not the whole solid, slide easily.

choices.text: Graphite reacts with metal surfaces to form a slippery carbide
choices.why: Graphite lubricates physically: its sheets slip past one another because the forces between layers don't vary much as they move.

explanation: Since the forces between the graphene layers do not vary much as the sheets move past one another, layer slip occurs easily, so graphite functions effectively as a lubricant. The same weak layering is what allows individual graphene sheets to be peeled off with scotch tape or chemical exfoliation.

prompt: The C–C bond length is 1.544 Å in diamond and 1.415 Å in graphite. By what percentage is the diamond C–C bond longer than the graphite C–C bond?
explanation: Percent longer = (1.544 − 1.415) ÷ 1.415 × 100% = 0.129 ÷ 1.415 × 100% = 9.12%. Diamond's bonds are pure σ single bonds, while graphite's have partial π character from its delocalized π network, so graphite's are shorter.

prompt: Why do fullerenes such as C60 undergo addition reactions readily, mainly at the C=C bonds joining two six-membered rings?

choices.text: Their carbons are bent toward a pyramidal shape to fit the curved cage, and addition relieves that strain by making a carbon tetrahedral
Their carbons carry hydrogen atoms that are easily substituted
choices.why: The carbons in fullerenes are all quaternary (no H), so they generally undergo addition, not substitution.

choices.text: They have no π electrons, so they behave like alkanes
choices.why: Fullerenes have a delocalized π system; that is why they are easily oxidized and reduced. Their addition chemistry is driven by strain in the curved cage.

choices.text: Their carbons are perfectly trigonal planar, as in graphite
choices.why: Planar graphite carbons are unstrained. In fullerenes the carbons must bend toward pyramidal to fit the cage's curvature, and that strain drives addition.

explanation: The carbons in fullerenes are all quaternary, so they generally undergo addition rather than substitution. To accommodate the concave cage, each carbon is bent slightly toward pyramidal, which creates considerable strain. Addition at a carbon makes it tetrahedral and relieves the strain, so fullerenes undergo nucleophilic and cycloaddition reactions, mainly at the C=C bonds joining two six-membered rings.

prompt: Carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5730 years, and the level of C-14 in an organism stops being replenished at death. What percentage of the original C-14 remains in a wood sample 17,190 years after the tree died?
explanation: 17,190 years ÷ 5730 years = 3.00 half-lives. The fraction remaining is (1/2)^3 = 0.125, or 12.5%. Comparing the C-14 to C-12 ratio with the atmospheric level is the basis of radiocarbon dating, useful for objects about 60,000 years old or less.

prompt: How does the stability of the carbon tetrahalides (CX4) change from CF4 to CI4, and why?

choices.text: It decreases, because the larger halogens overlap poorly with carbon's orbitals and crowd around the small carbon atom
It increases, because larger halogens form stronger bonds
choices.why: Bonds to carbon weaken as the halogen gets bigger. Poor orbital overlap and crowding make the larger tetrahalides less stable.

choices.text: It stays the same, because all are tetrahedral
choices.why: All CX4 are tetrahedral, but their stability decreases rapidly as the halogen grows.

choices.text: It decreases, because CI4 is not tetrahedral
choices.why: CI4 is tetrahedral, as VSEPR predicts. Its lower stability comes from poor orbital overlap and steric crowding.

explanation: The carbon tetrahalides all have the tetrahedral geometry predicted by VSEPR. Their stability decreases rapidly as the halogen increases in size because of poor orbital overlap and increased crowding. They are generally made indirectly, e.g., CH4 + 4X2 → CX4 + 4HX for X = Cl or Br, rather than from carbon and the halogen.

prompt: Why are fluorocarbons such as Teflon thermally and chemically more stable than the corresponding hydrocarbons?

choices.text: The C–F bond is about 25% stronger than a C–H bond
Fluorocarbons are ionic, so they don't react with organic reagents
choices.why: Fluorocarbons are covalent molecules and polymers. Their stability comes from the strength of the C–F bond.

choices.text: Fluorine atoms are smaller than hydrogen atoms
choices.why: Fluorine is larger than hydrogen. The key is the C–F bond, which is about 25% stronger than C–H.

choices.text: Fluorocarbons are much more hydrophilic than hydrocarbons
choices.why: Fluorocarbons have a hydrophobic character similar to hydrocarbons; their extra stability comes from the stronger C–F bond.

explanation: Because the C–F bond is about 25% stronger than a C–H bond, fluorocarbons are thermally and chemically more stable than the corresponding hydrocarbons, while having a similar hydrophobic character. Polytetrafluoroethylene is the nonstick Teflon lining of cooking pans.

prompt: Carbon monoxide reacts with chlorine to give phosgene: CO + Cl2 → Cl2C=O. How is this reaction best described?

choices.text: A redox reaction: Cl2, a two-electron oxidant, oxidizes the carbon of CO from +2 to +4
A Lewis acid–base reaction with no change in oxidation state
choices.why: That describes CO + BF3, which gives the adduct F3B:C≡O. With the oxidant Cl2, carbon is oxidized from +2 to +4.

choices.text: A redox reaction in which carbon is reduced from +2 to 0
choices.why: Chlorine is the oxidant here, so carbon is oxidized, not reduced: +2 in CO to +4 in Cl2C=O.

choices.text: An acid–base reaction in which CO donates a proton
choices.why: CO has no protons to donate. Its carbon is in an intermediate oxidation state and is oxidized by Cl2.

explanation: The carbon in CO is in an intermediate oxidation state (+2), so CO can act as a reductant or an oxidant, and it is also a Lewis base. Cl2 is an oxidant, so a redox reaction occurs: Cl2 is a two-electron oxidant and the carbon can be oxidized by two electrons to +4, giving phosgene, Cl2C=O.

prompt: CO is stable, but its sulfur and selenium analogues, CS and CSe, are unstable. Why?

choices.text: The C≡S and C≡Se bonds are much weaker than C≡O because of poorer π orbital overlap
Sulfur and selenium are more electronegative than oxygen
choices.why: Oxygen is the most electronegative of the three. The problem is weak π bonding: the larger S and Se orbitals overlap poorly with carbon's.

choices.text: CS and CSe would have an odd number of electrons
choices.why: CS and CSe have the same valence electron count as CO. Their instability comes from weak C–S and C–Se π bonds.

choices.text: Carbon cannot react with sulfur at any temperature
choices.why: Carbon reacts with sulfur at high temperatures, giving CS2. It's the triple-bonded CS that is unstable, due to poor π overlap.

explanation: The sulfur and selenium analogues of carbon monoxide, CS and CSe, are unstable because the C≡Y bonds (Y = S or Se) are much weaker than the C≡O bond due to poorer π orbital overlap. Heating carbon with sulfur instead gives only carbon disulfide, CS2.

prompt: Burning carbon gives ΔH = −110.52 kJ per mole of CO formed, or ΔH = −393.51 kJ per mole of CO2 formed. How much more heat, in kJ, is released when 36.0 g of carbon burns completely to CO2 rather than to CO? (Molar mass of C: 12.01 g/mol.)
explanation: Moles of C = 36.0 g ÷ 12.01 g/mol = 2.998 mol, giving 2.998 mol of either CO or CO2. Extra heat per mole of carbon = 393.51 − 110.52 = 282.99 kJ. Total extra heat = 2.998 mol × 282.99 kJ/mol = 848 kJ.

prompt: Which pairing of carbide type and example is correct?

choices.text: Interstitial carbide: tungsten carbide (WC), a hard, high-melting conductor used in cutting tools
Ionic carbide: silicon carbide (SiC)
choices.why: SiC is a covalent carbide: silicon's electronegativity is similar to carbon's. Ionic carbides come from electropositive metals such as group 1 and 2 elements and Al.

choices.text: Covalent carbide: calcium carbide (CaC2)
choices.why: CaC2 is an ionic carbide (an acetylide) containing Ca^2+ and C2^2− ions.

choices.text: Interstitial carbide: aluminum carbide (Al4C3)
choices.why: Al4C3 is an ionic carbide (a methide) containing the C^4− ion. Interstitial carbides come from transition metals.

explanation: Carbides fall into three classes. Electropositive metals (groups 1 and 2, and Al) give ionic carbides with discrete cations and carbon anions. Most transition metals give interstitial carbides with covalent metal–carbon interactions; these are good conductors, have high melting points, and are among the hardest substances known, e.g., WC for cutting tools and Fe3C in steel. Elements with electronegativity similar to carbon's give covalent carbides such as SiC and B4C.

prompt: Al4C3 contains the C^4− ion, while CaC2 contains the C2^2− ion. What gas does each give when treated with dilute aqueous acid?

choices.text: Al4C3 gives methane (CH4); CaC2 gives acetylene (C2H2)
Both give acetylene
choices.why: Only acetylides (C2^2−) give acetylene. The C^4− (methide) ion takes up four protons to give methane.

choices.text: Al4C3 gives acetylene; CaC2 gives methane
choices.why: It's the other way round. C^4− is derived from CH4 by removing four protons; C2^2− is derived from HC≡CH by removing two.

choices.text: Both give carbon dioxide
choices.why: Protonating a carbide anion gives the parent hydrocarbon, not CO2. CO2 comes from treating carbonates with acid.

explanation: Smaller metals such as Be and Al give methides like Be2C and Al4C3, which contain C^4−, formally CH4 that has lost four protons. Larger metals such as Na and Ca give acetylides like Na2C2 and CaC2, containing C2^2−, formally HC≡CH that has lost two protons. Dilute acid protonates the anions back to the parent hydrocarbons, CH4 or C2H2.

prompt: Miners' lamps burned acetylene made from calcium carbide: CaC2 + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + C2H2. What mass of acetylene, in grams, forms from 50.0 g of CaC2 with excess water? (Molar masses: Ca 40.08, C 12.01, H 1.008 g/mol.)
explanation: M(CaC2) = 40.08 + 2(12.01) = 64.10 g/mol, so 50.0 g ÷ 64.10 g/mol = 0.780 mol CaC2. The equation gives 1 mol C2H2 per mol CaC2, and M(C2H2) = 2(12.01) + 2(1.008) = 26.04 g/mol. Mass = 0.780 mol × 26.04 g/mol = 20.3 g.

prompt: Silicon dissolves in strong aqueous base, but the only aqueous acid it reacts with is hydrofluoric acid. What explanation does the section give?

choices.text: The formation of the stable SiF6^2− ion
HF is the strongest of the aqueous acids
choices.why: HF is actually a weak acid in water. Silicon reacts with it because of the stability of the SiF6^2− ion that forms.

choices.text: Silicon is a typical metal and dissolves in acids that oxidize it
choices.why: Silicon doesn't behave like a typical metal; it is amphoteric and resists most acids. Its reaction with HF is driven by forming SiF6^2−.

choices.text: Fluoride forms a protective coating that stops other acids
choices.why: A protective Pb^2+ salt layer is how lead resists acids. For silicon, HF works because the product SiF6^2− is very stable.

explanation: Based on its position in the periodic table, silicon is expected to be amphoteric. It dissolves in strong aqueous base to give hydrogen and silicates, but the only aqueous acid it reacts with is hydrofluoric acid, presumably because of the formation of the stable SiF6^2− ion. Silicon can expand its valence shell to six only with fluorine, since six larger halides can't fit around it.

prompt: How does the stability of the group 14 dichlorides (MCl2) change down the group?

choices.text: It increases dramatically: CCl2 is a short-lived intermediate, while SnCl2 and PbCl2 are stable solids at room temperature
It decreases: CCl2 is a stable gas and PbCl2 cannot be isolated
choices.why: The trend runs the other way. Dichlorocarbene (CCl2) can't be isolated, while PbCl2 is a stable, insoluble crystalline solid.

choices.text: It stays about the same, since all have the same formula
choices.why: The stabilities differ hugely: SiCl2 decomposes above −150°C, but SnCl2 is indefinitely stable at room temperature.

choices.text: Only CCl2 and SiCl2 exist; the heavier dichlorides are unknown
choices.why: All group 14 dichlorides are known, and the heavier ones are the most stable.

explanation: All group 14 dichlorides are known, and their stability increases dramatically with atomic number. CCl2 (dichlorocarbene) is a highly reactive, short-lived intermediate; SiCl2 decomposes rapidly above −150°C; GeCl2 is relatively stable below 20°C; SnCl2 is a polymeric solid indefinitely stable at room temperature; and PbCl2 is an insoluble crystalline solid. This matches the increasing stability of the +2 oxidation state from carbon to lead.

prompt: Lead reacts with chlorine to give PbCl2 rather than PbCl4. Why?

choices.text: Lead prefers the +2 oxidation state (Pb^4+ is a potent oxidant), and only fluorine is a strong enough oxidant to give lead(IV), as PbF4
Chlorine is a stronger oxidant than fluorine, so it stops at +2
choices.why: Fluorine is the stronger oxidant. That is why only F2 can take lead to the +4 state.

choices.text: Lead has only two valence electrons
choices.why: Lead has four valence electrons (6s2 6p2), like the rest of group 14. It prefers +2 because of the inert-pair effect.

choices.text: PbCl4 would be ionic, and lead forms only covalent compounds
choices.why: Lead is the most metallic member of the group. The issue is oxidation state: Pb(IV) is strongly oxidizing, so Cl2 gives Pb(II).

explanation: Although lead forms compounds in the +2 and +4 oxidation states, Pb^4+ is a potent oxidant (the inert-pair effect). Lead prefers +2, and chlorine is a weaker oxidant than fluorine, so PbCl2 forms. Only fluorine can oxidize lead to the +4 state, giving PbF4.

prompt: How does the acid–base character of the group 14 dioxides change down the group?

choices.text: They become increasingly basic, from acidic CO2 at the top to amphoteric oxides such as GeO2 and SnO2 further down
They become increasingly acidic, so the lead oxides are the most acidic
choices.why: Metallic character increases down the group, so the oxides become more basic, not more acidic.

choices.text: All are equally acidic, like CO2
choices.why: Only CO2, at the top, is classed as acidic. GeO2 and SnO2 are amphoteric, and basicity increases down the group.

choices.text: All are basic, since all group 14 elements are metals
choices.why: Carbon is a nonmetal and CO2 is an acidic oxide. Basic character grows only gradually down the group.

explanation: Consistent with metallic behavior increasing down the group, the dioxides of the group 14 elements become increasingly basic. CO2 is acidic, while GeO2 and SnO2 are amphoteric; for example, GeO2 dissolves in strong aqueous base to give an anion analogous to silicate.

prompt: Silica has the empirical formula SiO2, like CO2. What is its structure?

choices.text: A network in which each Si forms single bonds to four O atoms and each O bridges two Si atoms
Discrete linear O=Si=O molecules, like CO2
choices.why: Silicon forms four single bonds to oxygen rather than two double bonds, so silica is a network solid, not a molecular gas.

choices.text: Discrete SiO4^4− ions held together by silicon cations
choices.why: SiO4^4− is the building unit, but in silica the tetrahedra share all their oxygens to build a three-dimensional network.

choices.text: Layers of Si=O double bonds stacked like graphite
choices.why: Silica has no Si=O double bonds; every Si–O link is a single bond within a three-dimensional tetrahedral network.

explanation: Silica is not a silicon atom with two double bonds to two oxygens. Each silicon forms four single bonds to four oxygen atoms pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron, and every oxygen is bonded to two Si atoms. Averaged over the network, each Si has two O, giving the empirical formula SiO2. Quartz is pure SiO2.

prompt: In which class of silicate minerals does each SiO4 tetrahedron share all four of its oxygen atoms, giving a three-dimensional framework?

choices.text: Tectosilicates, such as quartz
Nesosilicates, such as olivine
choices.why: Nesosilicates are built from independent tetrahedra that share no oxygens; their charge is balanced by metal cations.

choices.text: Phyllosilicates, such as talc
choices.why: Phyllosilicates share three oxygens per tetrahedron, giving sheets, not a 3D framework.

choices.text: Inosilicates, such as pyroxenes
choices.why: Inosilicates share two or three oxygens per tetrahedron to form single or double chains.

explanation: Silicates are classified by how many oxygens each tetrahedron shares: nesosilicates share none (isolated SiO4^4−, e.g., olivine), sorosilicates are pairs sharing one O (Si2O7^6−), cyclosilicates form rings, inosilicates form single or double chains, phyllosilicates share three oxygens to form sheets (talc, micas), and tectosilicates share all four to form 3D frameworks (quartz, feldspars, zeolites).

prompt: A cyclosilicate ring is built from four SiO4 tetrahedra, each sharing two corners, giving the formula Si4O12. Treating Si as +4 and O as −2, what is the charge on the Si4O12 ring anion?
explanation: Charge = 4(+4) + 12(−2) = +16 − 24 = −8, so the ring is Si4O12^8−. The same counting gives −12 for the six-membered ring Si6O18^12− in beryl.

prompt: Zeolites are used in laundry detergents as water softeners. How do they work?

choices.text: Loosely bound Na^+ ions in the zeolite cavities are displaced by the more highly charged Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ ions of hard water, which bind more tightly
They oxidize Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ ions to insoluble oxides
choices.why: Ca^2+ and Mg^2+ can't be oxidized further. Zeolites exchange cations: they trade Na^+ for the more highly charged ions.

choices.text: They release Ca^2+ ions that precipitate soap
choices.why: Zeolites remove Ca^2+ from the water; they release Na^+ in exchange.

choices.text: Their Si–O bonds react with water to form silicic acid
choices.why: The zeolite framework stays intact. Softening comes from exchanging the loosely held cations in its cavities.

explanation: Zeolites are aluminosilicates whose 3D frameworks have large cavities joined by smaller tunnels. The cations in the cavities are readily exchanged, so in detergents the loosely bound Na^+ ions are displaced by the more highly charged Mg^2+ and Ca^2+ ions in hard water, which bind more tightly. Zeolites are also used as catalysts and for water purification.

prompt: Elemental silicon is made by reducing sand with carbon: SiO2 + 2C → Si(l) + 2CO. What mass of carbon, in grams, is needed to reduce 250. g of SiO2 completely? (Molar masses: Si 28.09, O 16.00, C 12.01 g/mol.)
explanation: M(SiO2) = 28.09 + 2(16.00) = 60.09 g/mol, so 250. g ÷ 60.09 g/mol = 4.160 mol SiO2. The equation needs 2 mol C per mol SiO2: 8.321 mol C × 12.01 g/mol = 99.9 g of carbon.

prompt: How do silanes (silicon hydrides) compare with their carbon analogues, the alkanes?

choices.text: They are much more reactive: SiH4 ignites on contact with air, and longer silane chains become less stable, unlike alkanes
They are more stable than alkanes because Si–H bonds are stronger
choices.why: Group 14 hydrides become less stable down the group. Silane ignites in air, while methane needs to be ignited.

choices.text: They are identical in reactivity because Si and C have the same valence configuration
choices.why: Despite the shared ns2 np2 configuration, silanes are much more prone to decomposition, especially by reaction with oxygen.

choices.text: They form stable Si=Si double-bonded analogues of alkenes
choices.why: E=E bonds weaken down the group, so Si=Si analogues of alkenes are unstable.

explanation: Unlike carbon, catenated silicon hydrides become thermodynamically less stable as the chain lengthens, and silanes are particularly prone to decomposition by reaction with oxygen. SiH4 ignites when it contacts air, being much more reactive than methane: SiH4 + 2O2 → SiO2 + 2H2O. The hydrides become less stable still down the group (SnH4 decomposes slowly at room temperature).

prompt: Tetraethyllead, (CH3CH2)4Pb, was once added to gasoline. Which statement about it is supported by the section?

choices.text: Its weak Pb–C bond breaks at low temperature to give alkyl radicals that control combustion, but it was banned largely because lead poisons catalytic converters
Its Pb–C bond is very strong, which makes it an inert fuel stabilizer
choices.why: The Pb–C bond is weak; that is exactly why tetraethyllead decomposes at low temperature to give alkyl radicals.

choices.text: Catalytic converters removed the lead it produced from exhaust
choices.why: Catalytic converters reduce CO, nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons but did nothing to decrease lead emissions; lead in fact poisons them.

choices.text: It contains lead in the +2 oxidation state
choices.why: Four ethyl groups are bonded to Pb, so lead is formally +4 in tetraethyllead.

explanation: The only important organic derivatives of lead are compounds such as tetraethyllead. Because the Pb–C bond is weak, they decompose at relatively low temperatures to produce alkyl radicals (R·) that control the rate of combustion. Burning them released lead oxide particles along highways, and because lead poisons catalytic converters, its use as a gasoline additive has been banned in most of the world.

prompt: Red lead, Pb3O4, can be viewed formally as lead(II) plumbate(IV), Pb2[PbO4], or 2PbO·PbO2. What is the average oxidation state of lead in Pb3O4?
explanation: Four O at −2 give −8, so the three Pb atoms together are +8, an average of 8/3 = +2.67. This matches the formal description of two Pb(II) and one Pb(IV): (2 × 2 + 4) ÷ 3 = 8/3. In nitric acid the PbO part dissolves as Pb(NO3)2 while the PbO2 part is left behind.
